Earl grew up in a house where love was measured in what got fixed and how little was wasted, and where nobody asked how you were doing because the answer was assumed from how hard you were working. When his grandfather died his junior year of high school, Earl spent three weekends in the garage sanding a cedar chest for his grandmother, delivered it without a word, and was told what a steady boy he was. He came out of that house knowing how to true a door and file a warranty claim, and having never once heard — or said — what a feeling was, out loud.

Precipitating. Three months ago, in late March, Earl's father died of a heart attack in his own driveway while clearing the last snow of the season — gone before the ambulance arrived, nothing said, nothing finished. Earl took one week off and has been at his desk every day since; what he stopped was everything else — he never bought his fishing license this spring, missing his first opener since he was eight, and the pine bookcase he was building for his father's fishing manuals sits half-sanded in the corner of his apartment.
